text: RLHF needs a reward: some function that looks at a generated SQL query and returns a number saying how good it is. For SQL Pete, that function doesn't come from a human rater reading thousands of outputs, and it doesn't come from a separate learned reward model either — it comes from actually running the query.

The idea is simple: execute the generated query against a sandboxed copy of Northwind or AdventureWorks2012, matching whichever schema the question targets, execute the gold query too, and compare the two result sets as unordered collections of rows. That gives a programmatic reward with no human rater needed at all.

But before any of that execution happens, every generated query passes through a hard safety filter. Only SELECT statements are allowed to run at all — anything destructive, like UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, or INSERT, is rejected outright, before it ever touches the sandboxed database, no exceptions.

Once a query clears that filter, it's scored on a fixed schedule: plus one point oh for an exact result-set match, plus zero point three for a partial overlap, minus zero point three for a syntax error or for running cleanly but returning the wrong rows, and minus one point oh for a disallowed statement caught by the safety filter.

That ordering matters. A reward-optimizing policy will find any loophole that scores well, so the safety rule doesn't just penalize destructive statements after the fact — it makes them structurally unreachable, by refusing to execute anything but a read-only query in the first place. That's the right way to think about alignment for a system with access to a real side effect.

This execution-correctness function is the entire reward signal for Project 3 — there's no separate learned reward model the way Project 2 trains one. Up next, Lesson 18: plugging it directly into TRL's PPOTrainer to run RLHF on SQL Pete.
